title: GhidraPT - AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering
description: Extends Ghidra with ChatGPT-powered code insights, accelerating reverse engineering by offering semantic suggestions and variable renaming.
role: I developed GhidraPT to streamline my own reverse engineering workflows and contribute to the cybersecurity tooling ecosystem. I designed the integration architecture, implemented the plugin, and tested it against several real-world binaries to fine-tune its relevance and responsiveness.
long_description: GhidraPT enhances the open-source reverse engineering tool Ghidra by integrating it with the ChatGPT API to analyze disassembled code and suggest more human-readable variable and function names. Built as an extension to Ghidra’s Data Manager functionality, the tool helps reverse engineers make sense of obfuscated or complex binaries more efficiently. Once installed, users can invoke AI-assisted analysis on selected symbols and receive recommendations in-line. This dramatically improves code comprehension speed, especially when dealing with unfamiliar binaries or stripped executables. GhidraPT demonstrates the power of augmenting static analysis workflows with natural language reasoning.
highlights: Extended Ghidra’s Data Manager with a custom plugin that integrates ChatGPT.
Improved reverse engineering speed with semantically meaningful variable renaming.
Enabled inline code understanding assistance within the Ghidra GUI.
Built with a modular interface to allow future integrations of other LLM APIs.
Open-sourced for the reverse engineering and infosec community to build upon.
insights: Working on GhidraPT sharpened my understanding of how static analysis tools can be paired with generative models to improve speed without compromising precision. It also deepened my appreciation for the limitations of LLMs when interpreting low-level code without context—and pushed me to build features that mitigate hallucinations through user oversight.

title: HybridRAG Oncology Research Assistant
description: An LLM-powered assistant that combines vector search and knowledge graphs to deliver explainable, grounded answers to complex oncology research questions.
role: I led the development of the HybridRAG Oncology Research Assistant, focusing on integrating hybrid retrieval mechanisms and ensuring the explainability of the AI-generated responses. My responsibilities included designing the system architecture, implementing the knowledge graph, and fine-tuning the language models for optimal performance in the oncology domain.
long_description: The HybridRAG Oncology Research Assistant is designed to support oncology researchers by providing accurate and explainable answers to technical questions. It integrates a hybrid retrieval system that combines dense vector search with structured knowledge graphs, enabling the assistant to retrieve relevant information from both unstructured and structured data sources. This approach enhances the explainability of the responses by allowing users to trace answers back to their sources within the knowledge graph. The system leverages large language models to generate responses that are both contextually relevant and grounded in verified data, facilitating more informed decision-making in oncology research.
highlights: Developed a hybrid retrieval system combining vector search and knowledge graphs for enhanced information retrieval.
Integrated large language models to generate contextually relevant and explainable responses.
Implemented a knowledge graph architecture to provide traceable and grounded answers.
Facilitated complex oncology research queries with improved accuracy and transparency.
Open-sourced the project to contribute to the research community.
insights: This project underscored the importance of combining unstructured and structured data retrieval methods to enhance the quality and explainability of AI-generated responses. By integrating knowledge graphs with traditional vector search, we achieved a system capable of delivering more accurate and transparent answers, which is crucial in the sensitive field of oncology research.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge Data Loss Prevention Solution
description: A lightweight data-loss-prevention firewall that screens user prompts before they reach an internal RAG LLM, catching corporate data-exfiltration attempts at the edge.
role: I designed and built this course capstone solo. I synthesized roughly 10k benign and malicious prompts with Gemini—grounded in a fictional corporate corpus plus red-team exfiltration scenarios so both classes were realistic—fine-tuned DistilBERT on that prompt set with the Hugging Face Trainer, and ran a head-to-head evaluation against Llama Guard 3 8B comparing accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and per-inference latency.
long_description: For the capstone of UT Austin’s applied machine learning sequence, I built a lightweight data-loss-prevention firewall that sits between users and an internal RAG LLM. Every prompt is screened before it reaches the model, catching corporate data-exfiltration attempts at the edge where they are cheapest to block. Because real exfiltration traffic is scarce, I synthesized roughly 10k benign and malicious prompts with Gemini, grounding them in a fictional corporate corpus plus red-team exfiltration scenarios so both classes were realistic. I fine-tuned DistilBERT on that prompt set using the Hugging Face Trainer, then ran a head-to-head evaluation against Llama Guard 3 8B—a purpose-built guardrail model an order of magnitude larger—comparing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 alongside per-inference latency. The result is a reproducible study of when a small, task-specific classifier can do the job of a frontier guardrail at a fraction of the cost.
highlights: Built a DLP firewall that screens user prompts before they reach an internal RAG LLM, catching exfiltration attempts at the edge.
Synthesized ~10k realistic benign and malicious prompts with Gemini, grounded in a fictional corporate corpus plus red-team scenarios.
Fine-tuned DistilBERT for sequence classification using the Hugging Face Trainer.
Benchmarked head-to-head against Llama Guard 3 8B on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and per-inference latency.
Produced reproducible evaluation artifacts—ROC curves and confusion-matrix analysis—comparing a lightweight fine-tuned model to a frontier guardrail.
insights: This project made concrete what I talk about in security work: the cheapest place to stop an attack is before it touches the expensive system. A small, task-specific classifier can match a much larger general-purpose guardrail on a narrow job while running far cheaper and faster at the edge—but only if the evaluation is honest about latency as well as accuracy, and only if the synthetic training data is grounded enough to survive contact with real traffic.

title: ALFRED - Local AI Assistant (IN PROGRESS)
description: A fully local, voice-controlled AI assistant that integrates LLMs, home automation, and tool orchestration via MCP.
role: I’m the sole designer and engineer of ALFRED, leading everything from architectural design to CUDA setup, speech integration, tool execution, and future RLHF training strategy.
long_description: ALFRED is an AI assistant designed for privacy, flexibility, and full offline control. It operates on my Ubuntu homelab system using a modular architecture that combines voice recognition, LLM inference, and a function orchestration framework (MCP). My voice commands are transcribed locally with whisper.cpp or Vosk, processed by a 30B LLM running via llama.cpp, and executed using custom local or remote tools. ALFRED can control Docker containers, manage homelab services, operate IoT devices via GPIO or SSH, and provide spoken responses via Coqui TTS or Piper. It’s designed to scale with federated tool discovery and is secured by VPN access. I'm also building persistent memory, RLHF feedback loops, multimodal vision, and a real-time web dashboard for total transparency.
highlights: Building a secure, fully offline voice-based AI system using GGUF LLM inference
Integrated STT, TTS, and Python orchestrator with model context protocol (MCP)
Exposed custom tools via FastAPI for IoT, file I/O, security camera analytics
Enabled GPU-accelerated inference of Qwen3-30B on local RTX 3090 system
Designed persistent memory system for RLHF and long-term customization
insights: Working on ALFRED has taught me how to coordinate multiple AI subsystems and low-level hardware control into a seamless, voice-first user experience. It's forced me to think deeply about orchestration, safety, auditability, and human feedback loops in AI systems.

title: Artificial Sunlight System
description: A modular IoT lighting system that simulates sunlight cycles and weather to support circadian rhythm health using MQTT and real-time control.
role: As co-creator, I led the system architecture design, MQTT communication stack implementation, power delivery engineering, and circuit safety. I also contributed to aesthetic design, soldering, and final presentation.
long_description: The Artificial Sunlight System is a suite of networked LED panels designed to replicate the sun’s natural radiance throughout the day. Built around ESP32 microcontrollers, RGBW LED strips, and a centralized MQTT server hosted on a Raspberry Pi, the system delivers programmable light cycles and ambient weather animations. The panels operate in a scalable, modular configuration—automatically adjusting behavior depending on how they’re connected (master/slave/pass-through logic). Real-time weather data is fetched and rendered across panels to visually simulate cloud coverage or other conditions for users without outdoor access. With applications in health, design, and DIY IoT networks, the project demonstrates how engineering can elevate quality of life by reinforcing biological cues like circadian rhythms, even in indoor environments. Modular design, open-source protocol stacks, and aesthetic attention to physical construction make this a true blend of engineering and creativity.
highlights: Implemented modular MQTT-connected panels capable of displaying artificial sunrise/sunset cycles and real-time weather animations.
Built a secure, remotely accessible IoT network using a Raspberry Pi as a centralized MQTT broker.
Designed scalable power and data protocols for dynamic multi-panel behavior (master, slave, pass-through).
Crafted custom enclosures using reflective acrylic and aluminum risers to combine thermal performance with aesthetic design.
Achieved panel brightness and color temperatures (1900K–8000K) sufficient to light an entire room and influence circadian response.
insights: This project pushed me to balance hard engineering constraints with human-centric design goals. I learned how to troubleshoot low-level power delivery, synchronize networked systems over MQTT, and refine a physical prototype that people actually want in their homes—not just use.

title: TALON - Offgrid Mesh Communication for Search and Rescue
description: An affordable, reliable LoRa mesh network designed to support search-and-rescue operations in infrastructure-poor environments like national parks.
role: As one of the lead engineers on TALON, I designed and built handheld communication devices, developed the backend integration with Meshtastic protocols, and co-led field validation trials. I also contributed to software engineering for the base station frontend and helped define system deployment strategies for rugged park environments.
long_description: TALON (Texas Aggie LoRa Outdoor Network) is a low-cost, offgrid communication system built to address the pressing need for reliable emergency communication in remote areas. Designed with national park visitors and SAR teams in mind, TALON uses Meshtastic-powered handheld devices to send GPS-tagged distress signals over LoRa mesh networks. These devices connect to repeaters and base stations—each designed for rugged conditions—to relay messages and location data to a centralized GUI for park staff. The full system includes custom firmware, durable 3D-printed enclosures, and a React-based frontend integrated with a Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL database. Through extensive field testing, TALON achieved 15+ miles line-of-sight communication and weeklong battery life, proving its viability for large-scale national park deployment with minimal infrastructure footprint.
highlights: Designed and built handheld devices, repeaters, and base stations using LoRa radios and custom firmware.
Implemented a live-updating React frontend for SAR teams, powered by a Supabase PostgreSQL backend.
Enabled off-grid GPS-based distress signal broadcasting with 15+ mile range under ideal conditions.
Field-tested devices in dense forests and elevated terrain to validate real-world performance.
Developed a rental-based distribution model for park visitors to ensure accessibility and affordability.
insights: TALON pushed me to bridge embedded systems with scalable cloud-based infrastructure, balancing hardware constraints with user-centered design. Building for real-world reliability in SAR contexts deepened my focus on security, resiliency, and testing—skills I now bring to every system I help design.
